extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners; organizational managers who oversee or interact with PR
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the role, structure, relationships, skills, and pitfalls of public relations functions within organizations, including internal departments and relationships with other units. Useful for designing PR departments, advising senior management, and integrating PR into strategic decision making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earn and hold top management support
rubrics_metrics.description: The first and continuing task for public relations is to earn and hold support from top management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop mutual respect with the CEO; strive to be the CEO’s 'loyal opposition' who can candidly advise against bad decisions behind closed doors. This relationship is critical to PR influence and requires time and credibility to establish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and perform the staff role
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations is typically a staff function that advises and supports line managers who have authority to run the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the line–staff distinction (line: product/profit functions; staff: advising/support). Staff should provide research, advice, and support without overstepping line authority—'on tap—not on top.' Explicit job titles (e.g., Staff VP/Director of PR) can clarify the role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity and access to decision makers
rubrics_metrics.description: Proximity to senior management and ready access to the CEO and dominant coalition increase PR participation in decision making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical placement near senior offices, frequent informal contact (hallway conversations, daily meetings) and visibility enable PR to influence judgment calls and policy setting. Example: moving PR offices to the same floor as senior management improved access during crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion in the dominant coalition
rubrics_metrics.description: PR has power when members of the organization’s dominant coalition (5–8 senior executives) value it as a vital management function rather than a technical implementer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure a 'seat at the table' so PR can help determine and achieve organizational outcomes. Demonstrable managerial value (not just technical skill) wins inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop strategic management skills
rubrics_metrics.description: To fulfill a strategic role, PR professionals need strategic management skills identified as evaluation research, environmental scanning, and research to segment publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build competencies in measurement, external environment analysis, and audience segmentation to move from tactical communication to strategic counsel (Excellence Project findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that organizational change affects PR influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational restructuring and reporting changes can enhance or diminish PR’s role in management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that reorganizations (e.g., creating executive councils or reassigning reporting lines) can either place PR closer to decision makers or bury it under other functions; adapt strategy and advocate for positions that preserve influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal credibility and practitioner characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners’ attributes—especially personal credibility—affect whether PR is included in the dominant coalition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of broad business experience, passivity, naiveté about organizational politics, overly technical backgrounds, gender, or short tenure can limit PR’s power. Invest in business knowledge, political savvy, and credibility-building activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct organizational intelligence and research
rubrics_metrics.description: Doing research ('organizational intelligence', environmental scanning, metrics) increases the likelihood PR will participate in decision making and planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular use of surveys, scans, and performance metrics demonstrates PR’s analytical value and supports strategic recommendations; labels vary but the practice is consistently linked to greater management inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage perceptions of PR by line managers
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which line managers and practitioners view PR as part of the management team determines PR’s role in decision making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If top management views PR as marginal, it will remain outside the decision-making coalition. Work to demonstrate strategic value and align PR activities with organizational priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in nonprogrammed decision making
rubrics_metrics.description: PR is seen as strategic when it participates in nonprogrammed (novel, complex) decisions rather than just routine, programmed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek involvement in high-level strategy and novel problem-solving to be perceived as contributing to organizational goals and the bottom line rather than merely overhead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use management by objectives (MBO) to focus on results
rubrics_metrics.description: When PR employs MBO (management by results), planning shifts from producing communications to achieving measurable results and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame PR programs with clear objectives tied to organizational goals so PR becomes accountable as part of the management team rather than only a producer of processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'seven deadly sins' of PR practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven behaviors threaten PR integration and credibility: (1) Overpromising, (2) Overmarketing, (3) Underservicing, (4) Putting the PR firm’s profits ahead of the client’s results, (5) Using PR quick fixes, (6) Treating PR as merely a support function executing others’ strategies, (7) Violating ethical standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of these practices to maintain trust with clients and top management; specific examples include promising outcomes you cannot deliver and using short-term fixes for complex problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help organizations adapt to environmental change
rubrics_metrics.description: As a management function, PR helps organizations identify, assess, and adjust to economic, political, social, and technological turbulence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position PR as a strategic sensing and adaptation function that informs policy and strategy, not just a communications executor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage team membership advantage of internal departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Being part of an internal department provides close team membership opportunities with management that support influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent contact with executives builds trust and positions PR as a key player; examples include daily meetings with CEOs and physical proximity to senior offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use insider knowledge advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal PR staff have intimate, current knowledge of organizational relationships, undercurrents, history, culture, and people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This insider knowledge enables continuous, context-aware advising, selection of credible spokespeople, and more efficient handling of routine and sensitive work compared with outsiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider economy/cost-effectiveness of internal departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal PR departments can be more cost-effective for ongoing programs due to lower marginal costs and better integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine activities and start-up project costs are often cheaper internally because staff already know the organization; weigh overhead and scale advantages against specialized outside expertise needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage availability and responsiveness of internal staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal staff availability offers rapid face-to-face response during crises and continuity for delicate matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proximity and on-call availability make internal PR valuable for urgent issues and for acting as deputies in sensitive situations; ensure role clarity to avoid misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against loss of objectivity in internal PR
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal department membership can erode objectivity as practitioners become too loyal or influenced by internal politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively protect outsider perspective, challenge groupthink, and maintain the ability to offer disinterested counsel to avoid becoming part of the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid domination, subservience, and role erosion
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal PR risks becoming co-opted into yes‑people, diverted to low-level errands, or viewed as replaceable technical support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define clear mission and roles, resist being used for unrelated tasks, and preserve strategic functions to prevent marginalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent confused mission and vague job descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Vague, open-ended job descriptions and overavailability can lead to accumulation of miscellaneous duties that undermine PR effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify responsibilities and protect time for core PR functions; example: a PR director assigned housekeeping duties lost time for publications and missed deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure appropriate department titles and reporting relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles vary (public relations, public information, public affairs, corporate communications), but the PR leader’s place on the org chart and reporting relationship to the CEO are more significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for direct reporting to the CEO or inclusion in the executive committee (C-suite) so communication impacts are considered during decision making; absence from the C-suite risks overlooking stakeholder effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate closely with marketing for integrated communications
rubrics_metrics.description: PR and marketing must work in harmony; confusion arises when PR is reduced to publicity or when marketing claims all goal-driven strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define responsibilities: product publicity supporting marketing vs advertising addressing broader public affairs. Coordinate messaging (avoid PR promoting 'green' commitments while marketing advertises non-green products). Integrated planning reduces turf battles and contradictory communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue functional integration where appropriate (PR and marketing)
rubrics_metrics.description: New structures integrate PR and marketing under unified leadership (e.g., CMO), blurring boundaries but offering opportunities for brand and relationship management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integration can work if leadership appreciates PR’s broader audience focus; be mindful that structural alignment alone doesn’t eliminate silos or budget conflicts—active coordination and shared KPIs are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate with legal counsel while respecting different perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal and PR counsel approach problems differently—lawyers favor caution/’no comment’ and adversarial representation; PR favors transparency and timeliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperate to protect legal interests while serving public information needs. Avoid misleading statements; PR professionals must never lie for a client. Coordinate especially during litigation, recalls, negotiations, and disclosures to balance legal risk and reputational impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate with human resources on employee communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential overlap exists when PR and HR address downsizing, crises, community programs involving employees, and internal communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work jointly on employee communication strategy during reorganizations and change management to ensure internal messages support external reputation goals and organizational culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate with IT on communication technologies and social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Advances in communication technology require PR to consult with IT to align platforms (email, websites, social media) with PR strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting IT manage social media as purely a technical platform; PR must shape message strategy and outcomes. Recognize different paces and priorities (IT emphasizes testing/stability; PR needs immediacy and responsiveness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Work with business intelligence/CPO on KPIs and performance monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaboration with business intelligence units and the Chief Performance Officer is important to define KPIs, benchmark progress, and tie PR to organizational performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Help identify stakeholders, determine relationship indicators, and communicate KPIs so all departments align on measures and can make strategic course corrections; up-to-date data supports timely managerial action.
